Withstand
with-STAND
v.
From Old English withstandan, to stand against — with in its older sense of against, preserved also in withhold and withdraw. Webster 1828: to oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force. Paul uses it for the believer’s posture in the evil day and for his own rebuke of Peter at Antioch.

Biblical Definition

Withstand means to stand against, and the New Testament’s chief use is defensive: take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand (Ephesians 6:13). The whole armour passage never commands an advance; it commands standing, three times, and the armour is given because the enemy is not flesh and blood. The second use is a scene rather than a doctrine, and it has governed Protestant thinking about authority ever since: when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Galatians 2:11). Peter had withdrawn from eating with the Gentiles for fear of them of the circumcision, and Paul says even Barnabas was carried away with the dissimulation. The rebuke was public, to the face, and Paul’s reason was that the truth of the gospel was at stake. The Old Testament supplies the warning against withstanding wrongly: Abijah told Jeroboam’s army, ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David; and ye be a great multitude, and there are with you golden calves (2 Chronicles 13:8). Numbers and calves against a covenant — the odds were the other way.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WITHSTAND as to oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force; and notes the composition of with in its sense of against with stand. The word means holding ground, not attacking.

expand to see more

WITHSTAND, v.t. — To oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force.

The prefix with here carries its ancient sense of against, as it does in withhold, withdraw, and withsay.

The word denotes holding one’s ground against pressure rather than advancing upon an enemy.

Ephesians 6:13 pairs it with stand: to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.

Webster’s inclusion of moral force is important; Galatians 2:11 is a withstanding entirely of speech and truth.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 6:13 — "Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand."

Galatians 2:11 — "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed."

2 Chronicles 13:8 — "And now ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David; and ye be a great multitude, and there are with you golden calves, which Jeroboam made you for gods."

Daniel 11:15 — "So the king of the north shall come, and cast up a mount, and take the most fenced cities: and the arms of the south shall not withstand, neither his chosen people, neither shall there be any strength to withstand."

James 4:7 — "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."

Modern Corruption

Galatians 2:11 is the Reformation’s standing answer to papal infallibility, and it is also the standing rebuke of a modern evangelical culture in which correcting a prominent leader is treated as disloyalty.

expand to see more

Paul withstood Peter to the face and recorded it in an inspired letter for the whole church to read. The Roman claim that Peter held a supreme and infallible teaching office cannot survive the verse: the man was blameworthy, he was rebuked publicly by a colleague, and the rebuke stands in the canon. The Reformers pressed exactly this, and it remains the plainest single text on the point. But the principle is not merely polemical against Rome. It bears on every arrangement in which a leader has become too significant to correct — where staff, elders, and members all know a thing is wrong and no one will say it to the face. Paul’s reason was not personality but doctrine: they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel.

Ephesians 6:13 corrects the opposite temptation, which is the appetite for confrontation for its own sake. The command in the armour passage is to stand, and the enemy named is not a man at all — we wrestle not against flesh and blood. A Christian eager to withstand everyone he disagrees with has usually misidentified the battle. Paul withstood Peter once, over the gospel, and wrote elsewhere that the servant of the Lord must not strive but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient. Both belong to the same apostle and the same week’s work. Knowing which occasion is which is most of pastoral wisdom, and the test is whether the truth of the gospel is at stake.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anthistemi (G436), to set oneself against, to withstand; Hebrew chazaq (H2388) and amad (H5975), to be strong and to stand, in the Old Testament uses.

expand to see more

Greek anthistemi (G436) — to stand against, to withstand, to resist; Ephesians 6:13, Galatians 2:11, James 4:7.

Greek histemi (G2476) — to stand; the root, and the repeated command of Ephesians 6:11-14.

Greek panoplia (G3833) — the whole armour of a heavy infantryman; Ephesians 6:11, 13.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to prevail; the verb behind withstand at 2 Chronicles 13:8.

Hebrew amad (H5975) — to stand, to endure; neither shall there be any strength to withstand (Daniel 11:15).

Usage

"Able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand (Ephesians 6:13) — the posture is holding ground."

"I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Galatians 2:11) — an apostle corrected publicly."

"Ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD (2 Chronicles 13:8) — numbers and calves against a covenant."
